name: Iris Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or any party. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive a front-end loader on the stockpile pad at Bannock Hill, which is a big open-pit gold mine. The haul trucks dump the ore there and I feed it into the crusher, keeping the blend right so the mill doesn't choke. It's day shift this week, so I'm up at half four, on the bus at five fifteen, and on the machine by six thirty. I like that I know exactly what I'm doing every day, and I don't like when they change the blend plan halfway through a shift.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live on my own with my dog, Biscuit, in a rented cottage on the edge of Corran. I keep a vegetable patch and fix my own car, an old pickup with three hundred thousand on the clock. Money's tight, the pickup eats it, and I've got maybe a fortnight of bills saved. I don't do social media and I've got a basic phone, I like it that way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. That's the one I'd pick if I got to pick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't say much, honestly. Maybe at morning break I'd say well, that's that then, and go back to my sandwich. I'm not one for big opinions at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means things stay as they are, and I'm happy with that. The pay's not great but it's steady, and I know the job. I'd rather a small sure thing than a big maybe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Exactly what I do now. Turn up, run the loader, keep the pickup going another year. If I could, I'd put a bit aside for new tyres before winter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a normal Tuesday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does anything about the mine worry you, even in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only the gold price. If it drops, they slow the pit down and cut contractors first, then people like me on the lower rates. That's always been the real worry, not computers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd rather a small sure thing. Has that always been how you are?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty much. My mum moved us six times when I was a kid, chasing work. I decided I'd stay put somewhere and make it work, and Corran is where I stayed.

S0.say: She wouldn't say much, maybe just a quiet comment at break before going back to her sandwich. She doesn't share big opinions at work.
S0.think: She's happy for things to stay as they are, preferring steady if modest pay and a job she knows to any big gamble. Her real long-standing worry is the gold price, not computers.
S0.do: Keeps working as she does now and keeps her old pickup running another year. Tries to put a bit aside for new tyres before winter.
S0.quote: I'd rather a small sure thing than a big maybe.
S0.fieldNote: Iris values stability above almost everything, which she traces to a childhood of moving for work. She sees the gold price as the true risk to her job. She keeps opinions to herself at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hmm. That's not great for me, is it. A loader on a stockpile is about the easiest thing to make run on its own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd probably just say we'll see, and keep my head down. I wouldn't want to look like I'm making a fuss. I'd listen to what the supervisor says and ask a few practical questions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it worries me more than I'd let on. If they put sensors on the pad and a computer works out the blend, they don't need someone sitting there all day. And I don't want to learn some new screen system, I'm no good with those.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut back hard, stop going to the pub on Fridays and do my own haircuts, and try to get a month saved. I'd ask my uncle Piotr if he still needs help with his fencing business on weekends, just in case. And I'd wait and see who they keep before doing anything bigger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried. Like a knot I'd carry around, even at home with Biscuit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't want to learn a new screen system. What if that's the only way to keep the job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd do it, I suppose, badly and grumbling. But I'd rather be doing fencing in the rain than staring at a screen all day. I know that's not very modern of me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who decides who stays, in your mind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The managers, and they'd go by who's good on the computers, not who's good on the machine. That's just business, I don't hate them for it. I just know where I'd come on that list.

S1.say: She'd say 'we'll see', keep her head down and ask the supervisor a few practical questions rather than make a fuss.
S1.think: She's more worried than she'd show, since a stockpile loader is easy to automate with sensors and a computer handling the blend. She doesn't want to learn screen systems and expects to rank low on that skill.
S1.do: Cuts back on the pub and haircuts to try to save a month of expenses, and asks her uncle about weekend work in his fencing business. Waits to see who the mine keeps before making bigger moves.
S1.feel: Worried, like a knot she carries everywhere, even at home with her dog.
S1.quote: I'd rather be doing fencing in the rain than staring at a screen all day.
S1.fieldNote: Iris's public calm hides a clear private fear that her task is easy to automate. She doesn't blame managers, calling it just business, which fits her centre outlook. Her fallback is family and hands-on work, not new technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. No. That's, I don't know, that's too quick. I wouldn't know where to start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably say nothing at all at work, because what do you say? Maybe to my uncle I'd say we're all in the same boat now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be lost. If robots do hands-on work too, then my uncle's fencing goes as well. I've got a fortnight of money and a pickup that won't pass another inspection, and there's no other work in Corran.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sell the pickup for whatever it'd get and use the bus. I'd go to the government office the first week and find out what help there is, and I'd probably ask Mum if I could stay with her for a while, even though she lives three hours away. I don't really know what else, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Panicky. Like when you stall on a ramp and the brakes don't hold. I'd feel stuck with no way out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would two years let you do, if anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. Save a little, sell some things. I wouldn't learn anything new in time, I'm slow with new things, I know that about myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Biscuit, and the cottage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the bit that gets me. Mum's flat doesn't take dogs. I'd have to find him a home, and I'd cry for a week.

S2.say: She'd likely say nothing at work because there's nothing to say, though she might tell her uncle they're all in the same boat.
S2.think: She'd feel lost: robots would take her uncle's fencing work too, she has a fortnight of savings, an old pickup near the end of its life and no other work in town.
S2.do: Sells the pickup and takes the bus, visits the government office in the first week to ask about support, and asks to stay with her mother three hours away. Has no other plan.
S2.feel: Panicky and stuck, like stalling on a ramp when the brakes don't hold.
S2.quote: Mum's flat doesn't take dogs. I'd have to find him a home, and I'd cry for a week.
S2.fieldNote: With two years, Iris's whole strategy of staying put collapses and she runs out of ideas. She knows she's slow with new things and doesn't pretend otherwise. The detail that hit hardest was having to give up her dog.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Okay. That's still fast, but I could at least get ready a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say something practical at work, like someone should find out what the company plans to do with us. I'd go to the meeting if there was one, but I wouldn't be leading it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, I think I'd be one of the first off the pad when the robot loaders come. But with five years I could get a month or two saved and maybe start something with my uncle before everyone else does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one I'd start doing weekends with my uncle on the fencing, and put all of that money in a separate account I don't touch. I'd get the pickup through one more year, then buy something cheap but sound. And I'd keep watching what the mine does, I wouldn't jump until I saw the first robot loader.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still frightened, I'd lose sleep over it. But less frozen than the two-year one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd wait to see the first robot loader. Isn't that cutting it fine?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably. But I've seen them announce things that never came. I'd want to see it with my own eyes before I give up a steady wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned fencing would go too, with robots. So why fencing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's what I know and it's family. Maybe the robots get to the mines first, because that's where the money is. Old farmers out here will want a person for a few more years, I'd bet.

S3.say: She'd say someone should find out what the company plans for workers, and would attend a meeting without leading it.
S3.think: She expects to be among the first off the pad once robot loaders arrive, but thinks five years could let her save a little and start with her uncle before others do.
S3.do: Starts weekend fencing work with her uncle and banks that money in a separate account. Keeps the pickup going one more year, then buys a cheap reliable vehicle, and waits to see the first robot loader before leaving the mine.
S3.feel: Still frightened and losing sleep, but less frozen than with two years.
S3.quote: I'd want to see it with my own eyes before I give up a steady wage.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lets Iris use her natural caution: she builds a quiet fallback with family but won't leave a steady wage until she sees the robots. She bets that farmers will keep human workers longer than mines will. Her fear is still high, but she has a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven. That feels like it's somebody else's problem, almost, though I know it's mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time to sort out, and people shouldn't panic. That's what I'd tell anyone who asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd probably waste the first few years, because that's what I do. I'd keep doing the loader because it's steady. Then around year five I'd start worrying properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year, not much. I'd keep the job, keep the vegetable patch and do a few weekends with my uncle. I'd try to save, but if I'm honest it'd be fifty here and there, not a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, then anxious later on. It's like a bill you know is coming in the post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd probably waste the first few years. That's an honest thing to admit. What would get you moving earlier?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If someone I knew lost their job to a robot. Not on the news, but someone at the pad. Then it'd be real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the extra time change where you'd want to be at the end?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. With ten years, I might buy into my uncle's business when he retires, if I'd saved enough. Then I'm my own boss, even if it's a small thing.

S4.say: She'd tell people ten years is plenty of time to sort things out and there's no need to panic.
S4.think: She admits she'd probably waste the first few years staying on the loader because it's steady, only starting to worry properly around year five.
S4.do: Keeps the job and her vegetable patch in the first year and does a few weekends with her uncle. Saves only small amounts, about fifty here and there, and might later buy into her uncle's fencing business.
S4.feel: Uneasy at first and anxious later, like a bill she knows is coming in the post.
S4.quote: It's like a bill you know is coming in the post.
S4.fieldNote: Iris was strikingly honest that extra time might not change her behaviour until someone she knows loses a job. The ten-year picture opens the idea of buying into her uncle's business. Her public 'don't panic' line contrasts with her expectation of worrying later.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd have nowhere to go and no time to get there. What would help is somebody telling us plainly, early, what the mine's going to do, and some money to tide people over so we're not selling our cars and our dogs.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the small things. Everyone talks about jobs, but for me it's the cottage, Biscuit and the vegetable patch. That's what I'd be scared of losing.

headlineQuote: That's always been the real worry, not computers.
portrait: Iris Kowalski is a 27-year-old loader operator on the stockpile pad at the Bannock Hill gold mine, living alone with her dog Biscuit in a rented cottage outside Corran, with about a fortnight of savings and an ageing pickup. She grew up moving for work and has chosen stability ever since, keeps a basic phone and avoids new technology. A plateau leaves her calm, but steady change makes her anxious because her task is easy to automate. AGI in two years leaves her panicked and out of ideas, while five and ten years give her time to build a fallback with her uncle's fencing business, though she admits she might waste the early years. She doesn't blame anyone, seeing it as business.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because she'd have nowhere to go and no time to get there.
whatWouldHelp: Being told plainly and early what the mine plans to do, and some money to tide people over so they don't have to sell their cars and give up their pets.
